SEP 2026 · Troubleshooting note

200 OK is not the outcome.

A successful request proves that one layer accepted something. It does not prove the customer experience worked.

Green transport can sit inside a broken journey.

An API can accept a syntactically valid request while the wrong identifier, stale field, incomplete consent state or unexpected data type sends the customer down the wrong path. The transport layer did its job. The business outcome still failed.

Technical success is only useful when it survives the full chain from source to customer outcome.

I troubleshoot the chain, not the tool.

TraceExpected → actual
Source→Ingestion→Identity→Profile data
Profile data→Eligibility→Journey→Channel / outcome

I start with the expected business behaviour and one known user or record. Then I move layer by layer until expected and actual diverge. That keeps the investigation evidence-based and prevents a tool, platform or team from becoming the default suspect.

Identity is a common hidden failure.

A backend event can land successfully while contact information, attributes or consent live on a different profile. From the API's perspective, everything worked. From the customer's perspective, nothing did.

That is why I treat identity separately from data ownership. “Who is this customer?” and “which system owns this fact?” are different questions, and both need explicit answers.

What I want before calling a fix done.

Known source record or event is correct
Intended identifier reaches the expected profile
Required attributes / events exist with the right types and freshness
Consent and channel eligibility are correct
Journey / automation logic evaluates as intended
Negative case fails safely
Monitoring can detect the same failure class again
An owner knows what to do when it happens

The practical rule.

Do not stop at “the API returned success,” “the file landed,” or “the campaign sent.” Those are checkpoints. The outcome is the intended customer behaviour, reached through a chain the team can observe and operate.

SEP 2026 · Practice note · integrations

Read the API docs before implementation.

The fastest integration debugging session is often the one that never happens because the team understood identity, limits, error behaviour and data contracts before writing code.

01 Why02 What I read03 Questions04 Payoff

Documentation is part of discovery.

Teams sometimes treat API documentation as implementation material for developers. I think it belongs much earlier. If the proposed design depends on an endpoint, event model, identity rule or rate limit, those constraints can change the architecture before anyone writes code.

A clean diagram built on an incorrect API assumption is still the wrong architecture.

The pages I care about first.

  • Authentication: how credentials are scoped, rotated and separated by environment.
  • Identity: which identifier is authoritative, whether anonymous and known profiles can merge, and what happens when identifiers change.
  • Request limits: payload size, batch size, rate limits and concurrency behaviour.
  • Error semantics: what a 200 actually means, which failures are retriable, and whether accepted requests can still fail later.
  • Data model: events versus attributes, required fields, timestamps and idempotency expectations.
  • Operational behaviour: logging, retries, webhooks, async processing and observability.

Questions I want answered before build.

Who owns the source of truth?
What identifier crosses the boundary?
What can arrive late or out of order?
What happens on duplicate requests?
How do we know the request actually worked?
What is the retry / recovery path?
What changes between dev and production?
What limit could change the design?

The payoff is not just fewer bugs.

Early documentation review makes requirements better. It exposes questions the business may not know to ask, gives engineering clearer acceptance criteria and helps the delivery team distinguish a platform constraint from an implementation choice.

It also makes trade-offs easier to explain. “The API cannot do that” and “we chose not to do that” are very different conversations.

SEP 2026 · Working style

Write down the decision, not just the meeting.

Meeting notes preserve conversation. Decision logs preserve what the team is now building against.

Teams rarely disagree about what was said. They disagree about what it meant.

A week after a meeting, one person remembers a recommendation, another remembers an approval and a third remembers an open question. Traditional notes can document all three interpretations without resolving which one governs the work.

The durable artifact is the choice: what we decided, why, who owns it and what would cause us to revisit it.

What I want in a useful decision record.

Decision logMinimum useful fields
FieldWhy it matters
DecisionStates the choice in plain language
AlternativesShows what was consciously rejected
RationalePreserves the constraint or goal behind the choice
OwnerMakes accountability visible
AssumptionsExposes what must remain true
Revisit triggerPrevents endless re-litigation while allowing new evidence

Decision logs are especially useful across system boundaries.

If marketing, data, architecture and development all leave a meeting with different assumptions about identity, source of truth or fallback behaviour, the disagreement may not appear until build or QA. A short written decision is cheaper than late rework.

The practical rule.

If a conversation changes architecture, scope, ownership, timing or customer behaviour, capture the decision separately from the meeting notes. The team should be able to find the current answer without replaying the meeting.

SEP 2026 · Technical note

Design the exit before the message.

A triggered journey is defined as much by what makes the message irrelevant as by what starts it.

The trigger is only half the business rule.

An abandoned search, incomplete application or cart event can justify a message. But the system also needs to know what should stop the message from being relevant.

If the customer books, buys, cancels, completes service or changes consent, the journey may need to exit immediately. Designing that condition late is how customers receive reminders for things they already completed.

For every trigger, ask which later event should make the trigger obsolete.

Exit logic protects relevance.

Journey patternExit condition
TriggerPossible exitWhy
Search abandonedBooking completedThe original intent has converted
Cart abandonedPurchase completedReminder is no longer relevant
Application startedApplication submittedNudge would contradict current state
Service reminderService completed / cancelledCustomer status changed
Any marketing journeyConsent revokedEligibility changed

Exit events also reveal architecture questions.

Where does the business know the customer completed the action? How quickly does that truth reach the engagement platform? Is the event server-authoritative? Can the journey react before the next message step?

Those questions often matter more than the creative because they determine whether the orchestration can stay aligned to reality.

The practical rule.

When designing a triggered journey, write the trigger and exit condition together. If the team cannot define the exit, the business rule probably is not finished yet.

SEP 2026 · Technical note

Events describe moments. Attributes describe state.

Lifecycle logic gets easier when transient behaviour and durable customer state are modeled differently.

Both can describe the same customer, but they answer different questions.

“Customer booked Paris” is a moment. “Customer has three lifetime bookings” is state. One is useful for triggering a journey around what just happened. The other is useful for segmentation and decisions that need the current truth.

Use events to remember that something happened. Use attributes to know what is true now.

Why the distinction matters.

If durable state is represented only as a stream of events, every downstream team has to reconstruct the current answer. If every moment is flattened into attributes, you lose useful sequence and timing.

ExamplesModel choice
DataShapeUseful for
Search abandonedEventTriggering a timely follow-up
Purchase completedEventConfirmation / post-purchase orchestration
Loyalty tierAttributeCurrent segmentation
Lifetime booking countAttributeEligibility / personalization
Last purchase dateAttribute derived from eventsLapse logic / reporting

Some data should exist in both forms.

A purchase can be an event because the moment matters, while lifetime purchase count and last-purchase date are durable state updated as a consequence. The mistake is assuming the same shape should serve every use case.

The practical rule.

Ask whether downstream users need to know that something happened, what is true now, or both. Model from that requirement rather than from whichever API field is easiest to populate.

SEP 2026 · Launch note

Go/no-go should be boring.

The final launch meeting should confirm evidence, not discover readiness.

A dramatic go/no-go usually means the real decisions happened too late.

If the final meeting is the first time the team asks whether audience counts reconcile, whether consent was tested, whether rollback exists or who is monitoring production, the problem is not the meeting. The control system failed earlier.

A good launch decision feels almost anticlimactic because the evidence already exists.

I want readiness to be observable.

“QA is good” is not enough. I want to know which scenarios passed, which risks were accepted, which version was tested and whether the production candidate is the same thing stakeholders approved.

Requirements accepted
Source data / audience reconciled
Consent and suppression tested
Negative cases passed
Release candidate frozen
Monitoring owner named
Stop / rollback path understood
Known risks explicitly accepted

The meeting should answer one question.

Given the evidence in front of us, are we comfortable putting this into production? If the answer depends on discovering new facts in the meeting, the launch is not ready for a decision.

This also changes escalation. A stakeholder can accept a known risk. They cannot meaningfully accept an unknown state.

The practical rule.

Define the proof before the build is finished. Then use go/no-go to review that proof, not invent it. The closer a team gets to launch, the fewer surprises the process should create.
